title: Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index (assume the end is always reachable).
shortTitle: Jump Game II: minimum jumps to reach the end (greedy BFS layers)

s1_definition.oneliner: Count a jump when the index reaches the current window boundary, then extend the boundary to the farthest reachable index, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Greedy layered BFS** – treat each jump as expanding a range; each jump is one BFS level from the current window to the farthest reachable position.
- **Current window boundary** – the rightmost index reachable with the current number of jumps; when the index reaches this boundary, a new jump is needed.
- **Farthest reachable** – as we scan within the current window, track the maximum of `i + nums[i]` to know how far the next jump can reach.
- **Iterate to n-2** – stop at the second-to-last index because reaching or passing the last index inside the final window already counts the jump.
- **Time O(n), space O(1)** – a single pass with three variables: jumps, end, farthest.
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India wants the fewest hops across settlement stages. Within one hop he can land anywhere in his current window. He scouts the entire window to find the farthest he could then reach, and only counts a new hop when he steps off the edge of his current window.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
     Jump Game II: Greedy Window Expansion

     nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]
     index:  0  1  2  3  4

     Window 0 (start): [0]
     ┌───┐
     │ 0 │  farthest = 0+2 = 2
     └───┘
     i == end => jump! jumps=1, end=2

     Window 1 (jump 1): [1, 2]
     ┌───┬───┐
     │ 1 │ 2 │  farthest = max(1+3, 2+1) = 4
     └───┴───┘
     i == end => jump! jumps=2, end=4

     end=4 >= last index (4) => reached!

     Result: 2 jumps

     BFS equivalence:
     Level 0: {0}         0 jumps
     Level 1: {1, 2}      1 jump
     Level 2: {3, 4}      2 jumps  <-- 4 is the target
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game II asks for the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index, and the optimal solution is a greedy window expansion that compresses a BFS into three variables. The current window boundary marks the rightmost index reachable with the current number of jumps. As we scan left to right, we track the farthest reachable index. When the scan position reaches the window boundary, we must take a new jump and move the boundary to the farthest.

The critical detail is iterating only to the second-to-last index. Reaching or passing the last index inside the final window already counts the jump, so including the last index in the loop would overcount by one. The time is O(n) and the space is O(1).

The greedy works because extending to the farthest reachable within each window is equivalent to BFS level processing, and BFS gives the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Each window is one BFS level, and because we always take the widest window, we use the fewest levels.

At National Bank of India, a courier crossed settlement stages and needed the fewest hops because each hop carried a fixed handling cost. The greedy window expansion gave the minimum hops in a single linear pass. The DP alternative with dp[i] = minimum jumps to reach i is O(n squared), which Rajesh avoided by recognising the BFS structure.

Remember one sentence: count a jump when the index hits the current window boundary, extend the boundary to the farthest reachable, and stop at n-2 to avoid overcounting.

---

keyPoints: Track three variables: jumps counted, current window boundary (end), and farthest reachable index.
When the scan index reaches end, increment jumps and move end to farthest: one new BFS level.
Iterate only to nums.length - 2 to avoid overcounting; reaching the end inside the window already counts.
Time is O(n) with O(1) space: a single pass with three variables replaces a full BFS queue.
Greedy correctness comes from always extending to the farthest reachable within each window, equivalent to BFS.
The DP alternative dp[i] = min jumps to reach i is O(n squared); the greedy avoids that by using window boundaries.
